en: When the Buddha preached the *Dharmarāja-sūtra*, from within that radiance... [the] Bodhisattva...
immediately rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to stand to one side. Five...
He prostrated himself on the ground, weeping with tears streaming down his face, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Honored One among Gods!
The Tathāgata intends to enter parinirvāṇa; the time is drawing near."

If, fifteen hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, sentient beings in the five turbidities commit many evil deeds and practice exclusively the ten non-virtues, such beings will have weak power of merit. Regarding the profound and wondrous Dharma of the twelve divisions of the scriptures spoken by the Buddha—its vast texts and extensive meanings being difficult to understand—they will be unable to grasp or comprehend that Dharma.

I pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will expound the definitive truth of the Mahāyāna, so that these sentient beings may obtain the truly wondrous medicine to cure all diseases of poison, and may all be brought to complete healing.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!”
That you are able to ask such a question for the sake of all sentient beings will bring inconceivable and great benefit.
I shall now, for your sake, analyze and proclaim the definitive meaning of the true Mahāyāna.

Why is this? It is for the sake of delivering sentient beings, causing all sentient beings to leave behind afflictions, leading them out of the suffering of hell to be born in a pure land, and ensuring their certain liberation and transcendence of birth and death.
"You all should be single-minded; I shall proclaim it for you.
At that time, the great assembly was filled with immense joy and leaped for gladness; with one voice and in unison, they cried out:
"We pray that the Buddha, out of his compassion, will proclaim it for us."
The Buddha said, "O sons of good family!

Those who seek liberation should sever all攀缘 (pān-yuán, objective attachments). With single-mindedness and no duality, they should relinquish the marks of a mind that exists; for the essence of the mind-nature is empty. Within this mind-nature, there is neither defilement nor relinquishment."
If there is neither grasping nor rejecting, then there is nothing to be attained;
if there is nothing to be attained, that is called bodhi. Why is this?
The multitude of afflictions all arise from the single mind; if the mind does not arise, afflictions do not arise. Regarding the wisdom of all objects, there is then neither grasping nor rejecting.
If there is no grasping or rejecting, one is detached from all attachments;
if one is detached from all attachments, one does not engage in objective conditions.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The cognitive faculty regarding the realm of sentient beings can give rise to both good and evil.”
"This is the locus of dependent origination, wherein all phenomena of the two extremes—internal and external—interpenetrate one another.
How can one remain within this without grasping or rejecting?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:
“Good son! In the first dhyāna-aggregate, one contemplates that both the internal and external are ultimately non-existent. Why is this?
Contemplating the internal, one finds that the true nature does not arise; contemplating the external, one finds that ignorance does not occur.
Where there is neither arising nor occurrence, there is no nirvana; this is purity, this is the wondrous and excellent medicine.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

The true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Mahāyāna spoken of by the Tathāgata is profoundly deep and subtle; it is the unsurpassed, excellent medicine that enters the truth of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Yet, sentient beings have impurities in their three karmas, commit the ten unwholesome deeds, and practice the conduct of those who have abandoned all hope (*icchantika*); their faculties are narrow and inferior, making it difficult to apply the medicine of the mind according to the distinctions between ailments. By what skillful means can they be led to enter the Mahāyāna?”
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja:
"I possess a skillful means that causes one to enter the Mahāyāna.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

From of old I have heard that the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma of the six pāramitās for those of the Great Vehicle, the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination for those of the Middle Vehicle, the Dharma of the four noble truths for those of the Small Vehicle, and the Dharma of the ten wholesome actions for icchantikas; in each case, he administers the appropriate medicine according to the specific ailment.”
"Why do you say today that you preach the Dharma of the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna) to save these four types of people?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha:

"When I speak of the path of the Single Vehicle, it is like the single earth which can produce all things and nourish everything; it is like a great rain that universally moistens all things, so that whatever grows upon the earth receives its moisture."

It is like rice of a single grain or a meal of a single flavor; all beings in the world, whether humans or non-humans, take it as food, and those who eat it are all able to nourish their bodies and sustain their lives.

It is like a medicinal king that skillfully compiles an exquisite elixir: those with feverish ailments who consume it find coolness; those with cold ailments who consume it find warmth; those suffering from diarrhea find it immediately stops; those suffering from constipation find it immediately clears; there is no illness that it does not cure.
"I preach the Dharma of the One Vehicle to those four types of people; my healing of all their ailments is likewise so.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"By what skillful means can those sentient beings who commit the ten evils and are icchantikas be led to enter the path of the One Vehicle?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha: "Good son!"
My One Vehicle Dharma already encompasses the Three Vehicles; there is no separate teaching that establishes the Three Vehicles as distinct.
Listen attentively, and I shall proclaim it for you. "Good son!

The wondrous Way profoundly embodies the single mark of non-duality; yet, for the sake of skillful means, it is taught as the three vehicles. All dharmas and the three vehicles accord with this single contemplation, and although sentient beings are of four types, they likewise possess no duality regarding their Buddha-nature.

Why is this? All Buddhas and all sentient beings share the same nature and characteristics, being of one essence without distinction; it is only the minds of sentient beings that give rise to conceptual discrimination.

The Buddha is sentient beings, and sentient beings are the Buddha. All sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature; the Buddha-nature and the nature of sentient beings are of one and the same nature. Because this single nature is equal to all dharmas, I employ skillful means to lead them into the One Vehicle.

“Good son! Cause those sentient beings to fortify the city of their minds so that the thieves do not enter through the great gate of the six consciousnesses. Guarded by the vajra, they should dwell in the abode of contemplating the mind and know the abode where the mind dwells; yet within that very abode of the mind, they do not dwell upon the mind.”
If the mind does not abide, then the mind remains unestablished;
by not abiding in various evils or sensory objects, one ceases to engage in objective grasping (*ālambana*);
because one is free from such grasping, the mind becomes devoid of seeking.
If the mind has no seeking, the mind has no dwelling;
if there is no place of dwelling, it is called the truly dwelling mind. "Good son!
The minds of sentient beings give rise to all manner of afflictions because they are produced by the mental consciousness and do not abide.
If that mind were to abide, there would be no afflictions;
if there are no afflictions, that is itself bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when all sentient beings give rise to various afflictions and their minds do not abide, by what power do they arise and engage in objective apprehension?”
"I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain this for the sake of the assembly. The Buddha said:
"All sentient beings produce various dependent originations through two types of power."
What are these two? First, that which arises conditioned by external objects; this is the power of conditions.
Second, that which arises from one's own mind independently, without relying on external objects; this is the power of nature.
Good son! To cause all sentient beings not to give rise to the duality of natures means that there is neither affliction nor bodhi.
If there is neither affliction nor bodhi, one enters the realm of reality; this is true bodhi.
"You bodhisattvas, when transforming sentient beings, should cause their minds to abide [in suchness].
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"You transform and deliver sentient beings, causing their minds to abide; abiding in what place do they attain bodhi?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! You have asked well regarding the meaning of this mind, which is inconceivable even for great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Listen attentively, and I shall explain it to you."
Good son! If you transform sentient beings so that their minds abide, that abiding is not within, it is not without, and it is not in between;
the Dharma-vehicle of all Buddhas likewise is not within, nor is it without, nor is it in between.
Abiding with a single-minded spirit in a state of non-abiding, one thus attains bodhi.
If one attains bodhi, there is likewise no bodhi to be attained; this is called suchness (tathatā).
Why is this? Because afflictions arise delusively and are thus empty of delusion;
because all phenomena do not arise of themselves and are thus empty of phenomena.
This mind possesses only a mere name; the mind itself cannot be apprehended, for the mind is also empty.
Sons of good family, if you know that the mind is empty, you should not falsely perceive all things within this single empty mind.
If you perceive all things, it is called the defilement of the mind.
"If the defilements of the mind are absent, it is called the exhaustion of outflows; the eye, forms, and the mental element—these three are eternally pure as emptiness.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"

If all phenomena were thus, then all sentient beings should be able, within a single body, a single mind, and a single world, to enter a single Buddha-world, and from that single Buddha-world, to enter all Buddha-dharma worlds that pervade empty space.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja: “Good son, it is so, it is so.”

All worlds enter into a single world; within each and every world is a lotus throne, and within each and every lotus is a Tathāgata seat. Each and every Tathāgata body fills all worlds, manifesting that all worlds are entirely empty space.
The Buddhas adorn all worlds, and there is a single body of each and every bodhisattva that fills all worlds. Possessing great supernormal power, they place all worlds within a single pore;

all worlds enter the body of a single sentient being, with the number of worlds equal to the number of bodies of each individual sentient being. Each world is a single Buddha, and at each Buddha’s site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is a single Bodhi tree. Beneath each Bodhi tree is a seat for a Buddha, and a single Buddha-body fills all worlds. The sublime voice of each Buddha also fills all worlds, so that in every world, according to what is appropriate, there is none who does not hear and understand, and all are filled with joy.

“O practitioners, you should know that the Dharma resides within your own bodies; you ought not to seek the Buddha-body in all other worlds and places, but rather seek the Buddha-body within a single mind and a single world.”
Within a single body one can produce all bodies, and within all bodies one can produce a single body.
Why is this? Because a single body is the body of a Buddha.

The bodies of all sentient beings, as well as the bodies of all sentient beings and the bodies of all Buddhas, are all born from the one mind. If the one mind is good, all phenomena are entirely good; if the one mind is evil, all phenomena are entirely evil. If one performs evil karma, one is born with the body of an evil sentient being; if one performs good karma, one is born with the bodies of devas, humans, or other beings. If, within the one mind, one is detached from the thoughts of the one mind, and within the characteristics of the mind finds nothing to be grasped—furthermore, detaching from the realm of emptiness at the ground of non-apprehension—one can give birth to the Buddha-body.
Within the Buddha’s body, there is but one body without duality, because there is but one Buddha-nature.
Within this one Buddha-nature is the one mind-nature; outside of this one mind, there is nothing else to be sought. To seek anything else would constitute a perversion.

Why is this? All mental phenomena have no basis for being requested from without; that which is sought from without is precisely what is called "other," and to seek from another is to fall into falsehood.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since one attains Buddhahood within a single moment of mind, there is the Buddha-nature within all moments of mind; all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.”
"If each and every one can stabilize their body and mind, they will immediately attain Buddhahood; apart from this, there is no other place to seek Buddhahood.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, saying: "Good son!
So it is, so it is. Just as you have said, all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

All Buddhas and Tathāgatas, by means of the Dharma of the single mind, cause all sentient beings and all their minds to seek the Buddha-dharma within the single mind and thereby attain the Buddha-body.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature and seek to attain Buddhahood within that Buddha-nature, and since all sentient beings possess a mind and likewise possess the Buddha-nature, then this [Buddhahood] is obtainable and it is visible.”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying: “Good son!
When entering the juncture of the Buddha’s wondrous nature and true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa), it is neither obtainable nor unobtainable, and neither visible nor invisible.”
Why is this? If a bodhisattva says that the Buddha-nature exists, it is called slandering the Buddha;
if they say that the Buddha-nature does not exist, it is likewise slandering the Buddha.
To say that the Buddha-nature both exists and does not exist is also to slander the Buddha;
to say that the Buddha-nature neither exists nor does not exist is also to slander the Buddha. Why is this so?
Bodhisattvas, sentient beings, and the Buddha-nature do not exist like empty space, nor are they non-existent like the horns of a rabbit;
for while rabbit horns do not exist, empty space is eternal.
It possesses no characteristic of substantiality, nor does it possess the characteristic of emptiness; it is free from all forms and signs because it is without attachment.
It does not abide in the place of arising, and for this reason it is not defiled; it does not dwell in the place of cessation, and for this reason it is not severed.
The wondrous characteristics of the Buddha-nature of sentient beings are thus: to say that the Buddha-nature exists is the slander of exaggeration;
to say that the Buddha-nature does not exist is the slander of deprecation;
to say that the Buddha-nature neither exists nor does not exist is the slander of conceptual proliferation.
"To say that Buddha-nature is both existent and non-existent is a contradictory slander.
Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
If the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is thus wondrous, being free from all realms and therefore unstained— just as the nature of empty space is eternally pure—
how is it that sentient beings produce various afflictions?
If one generates a mind of affliction, it is defilement.
From what does this defilement of the mind arise?

We only pray that the World-Honored One will proclaim this for the sake of the assembly, so that all sentient beings may hear and know it; and so that all sentient beings may shatter their afflictions, cleanse the defilements of the mind, and forever leave behind the hindrances and entanglements.
The Buddha immediately smiled with joy and, stroking the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head with the palm of his left hand, emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated all things.
At that time, the great assembly and all sentient beings were filled with immense joy and leaped for gladness.
The Buddha said:
“When a bodhisattva asks such questions on behalf of all sentient beings, this is called a correct question; it delivers sentient beings.
If one asks other kinds of questions, this is called a deviant question; it destroys sentient beings.”
"O Bodhisattvas!

You have asked this question correctly for the sake of delivering sentient beings. All of you, sentient beings, should listen attentively with single-minded focus, setting aside all distracted thoughts and ceasing all external preoccupations, remaining firm in your resolve."
"I shall proclaim it for you; if any hear this teaching, all sentient beings who have committed the ten non-virtuous actions will attain liberation.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“We, this great assembly, and all sentient beings, with one mind and without any further distracted thoughts, pray only that the World-Honored One will proclaim the teaching for us.
The Buddha addressed the assembly of Bodhisattvas and others:

“All afflictions arise from inversion; all inversions arise from false conceptualization; all false conceptualizations arise from the notion of self; all notions of self arise from the rootless; and this rootlessness is precisely non-abiding.”
That which is without abiding and without origin is non-existent;
existence is defilement, while non-existence is purity.
Within this state of purity, there is the perfection of permanence, the perfection of bliss, the perfection of self, and the perfection of purity.
If one holds such a view, it is called right view;
if one holds any other view, it is called wrong view.
One who sees in this way is a person possessed of wisdom.
Those who hold such views lack wisdom.
If one possesses wisdom, then they are liberated through skillful means;
if one lacks wisdom, then they are bound by skillful means.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings in a pure place who constantly give rise to the perception of permanence, the perception of pleasure, the perception of self, and the perception of purity, they possess wisdom; they are not inverted.”
The Buddha said, “Bodhisattva!
If there are sentient beings who have such a conception, it is called right conception; such a person has right view, and such a person possesses wisdom.”

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is the perfection of permanence, the perfection of bliss, the perfection of self, and the perfection of purity. One who perceives the pure abode of the Buddhas’ Dharma-body in this way is a true and singular disciple of the Buddha; born from the True Dharma, transformed by the Dharma, and born from the Buddha’s own mouth, such a person attains the four reliances of the Buddha. Although they are called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they are a Bodhisattva of the four reliances.

"Good son! After my parinirvāṇa, whether it be five hundred years, a thousand years, or fifteen hundred years hence, if there should be someone who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sutra as taught, possessing faith and right view regarding the state of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and furthermore teaches this Dharma to even a single sentient being, such a person is called a bodhisattva. Although they may be called an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), they are worthy of receiving offerings and are a renunciant."
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As for one who has left the household life, having shaved off their hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, upholding the complete precepts and remaining unstained by the secular world—this is called ‘leaving the household life,’ and such a person is worthy of receiving offerings.”
The Tathāgata has now stated that ordinary persons are renunciants who may receive offerings, yet we do not understand the meaning of this.
We pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will explain it for us.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:
"Good son! Those who shave off their hair and beard do so to eliminate the notion of self-identity and to subdue the body through non-self."
Wearing the dharma robes with a straightforward mind free from flattery and crookedness, and because they desire to leave the mundane world;
those who maintain the complete precepts and do not give rise to greed, anger, or delusion—
I say that such persons are called "those who have left the home life."

Although he is an ordinary person, he is able to subdue body and mind so that pride does not arise; his heart is unstained by worldly dust, and having long since departed from the mundane mind, his indestructible nature of precepts is like a diamond—thus, though an ordinary person, he is a true renunciant.

Furthermore, within these Mahāyāna sūtras of this teaching, they practice according to what is taught; because they have faith in the Buddha’s words, they perceive permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and proclaim them for the sake of sentient beings. Although they are still ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), they are persons of the four reliances (*catur-apaśraya*), are practicing bodhisattvas, and are worthy of receiving offerings; they are called "practitioners" (*yogin*).

Having attained wisdom and skillful means, one preaches the Mahāyāna Dharma; such dharmas of nature are all inseparable from the mind, born through transformation from the mind, serene and eternally uniform, a single mark without duality. Within this single mark, there is neither interior nor exterior, nor even a middle, for it is free from all things.
If one is detached from all things, there is neither arising nor ceasing;
that which is without arising or ceasing is precisely True Suchness (Tathatā).
True Suchness is eternally abiding, and while the Dharma and the Sangha do not perish, the sentient beings of the three realms are born and die of their own accord.
"Good sons! Therefore it is said that sentient beings have no self, while the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the true self, for they are able to shatter the flow of birth and death.
You sentient beings!"
"If one seeks the eternal and abiding, one should depart from all desires and practice the conduct of non-arising.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"What kind of practice is called the 'practice of non-arising'?
The Buddha said,
"O sons of good family!..."
If I do not give rise to another, then another does not give rise to me.
Why is this? Because their essential nature is pure emptiness, neither existent nor non-existent, and eternal.
All objects are empty and pure; they are neither non-existent nor subject to cessation.

Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas constantly use the incense of a single flavor and a single nature to permeate the one-mind-nature of all sentient beings. Thus, those who possess wisdom attain the realization of emptiness, while the ignorant enter into delusion and the bonds of attachment.

Why is this? Because wise sentient beings are free from delusion; regarding the nature of awakening, they awaken to the non-arising of all ignorance. Being without [dualistic] awakening, they are neither empty nor fixed, entering a single purity forever free from all afflictions.

Because foolish sentient beings possess ignorance, they fail to awaken to the nature of existence within the state of being; thus, they give rise to non-awakening and create the afflictions of various sensory objects.
If there is awakening, then there is no non-awakening;
if there is no non-awakening, then illness does not arise.
If illness does not arise, then there is no perception.
If there is neither perception nor non-perception, then there is no deluded mind. Why is this?
First, because the doubting mind contains two intentions:
if there is no doubting mind, then illness does not arise;
if there is a place where [the mind] arises, it enters an empty house.
The single nature is true emptiness; conditioned phenomena are signless. When encountering objects, they arise through conditions like illusions or transformations in space.

The Bodhisattva causes all sentient beings to sever their doubting minds, acting as masters of their own minds rather than being masters of the mind, remaining free from all desires and ensuring they do not become negligent.

If a thought arises in the foundations of mindfulness, it must be immediately severed. When the preceding thought and the succeeding thought do not conflict with one another, one attains accord with principle and does not give rise to ignorance; this is because awareness is not fixed and its essence is fundamentally unmoving. Thus, when a thought arises, one should still the thought that has already arisen.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if thoughts from the past arise, by practicing what dharma can one awaken to them and bring them to cessation?”
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva causes all practitioners to observe the dwelling place of the mind at every moment; by knowing the dwelling place of the mind, one does not dwell upon the mind.
Because of this awakening, one brings it to rest through that very awakening; when the desire for thought does not arise, there is then neither cessation nor contemplation.”

If there is an arising, it abides in emptiness; within the single nature of emptiness, both defilement and purity are extinguished. Its self-nature is pure, neither grasped nor abandoned, such that even mindfulness does not arise. There is no birth and no activity; the sphere of mental activity is extinguished and the path of language is cut off.
The single Buddha-nature is awakening; there is no other awakening. This wondrous nature exists eternally like empty space, unattached to anything.
If a bodhisattva practices this way, it is like wielding a staff to strike at empty space—neither stained nor attached. This is called the practice of the Dharma.

If there is any place of defilement, one immediately enters the realm beyond the mundane; wandering through the pure ground with single-mindedness and non-duality, one enters the samādhi of the true nature, contemplates the single ultimate truth, and thereby performs repentance.

At that time, there was among the assembly a person of the *icchantika* class named Many Desires (*Bahukāma*). Since ancient times, he had committed many evil deeds and was solely devoted to the ten unwholesome actions; he was dragged along by the four snakes of hatred, anger, jealousy, and envy, and his very root of mind was gnawed away by the two rats of false conceptualization.
It is like a person suspended from a tree by a rope, with four snakes below spitting venom toward him, while two rats on the tree gnaw at the rope, intent on severing it.
If the mind ceases, then the three karmas are purified;
if the mind does not cease, then the eye, forms, and the mind together constitute delusive conceptualization, and being bound by such views, one is about to fall into hell.

At that time, because the icchantika had heard the Dharma from the Buddha, a sense of shame and remorse arose in his mind for a single thought-moment; he wished to ask the Tathāgata about the method of repentance, yet harboring such shame and remorse, he was unable to pose the question.

The Tathāgata, through his supernormal powers, immediately knew their thoughts and, wishing to cause these people to be free from all suffering and distress and to emerge from the gates of hell, spoke to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha:

"After my parinirvāṇa, if there are icchantikas who commit many evil deeds—extinguishing the Three Jewels of the Buddha, slandering the True Dharma, and committing the five heinous crimes—they will certainly fall into the various hells, remaining there for as long as twelve great kalpas without being able to escape."
“You bodhisattvas should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, causing these sentient beings to confess their transgressions so that they may all attain liberation.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!...”
"By performing what dharma can one repent and eliminate the offense?
We pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will explain this for us. The Buddha said:
“If a bodhisattva wishes to repent, they should contemplate the True Reality (satyadharma). If one perceives the True Reality, all transgressions will be entirely eliminated.

After the Buddha had spoken these words, at that time, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings among the assembly—both humans and non-humans—all single-mindedly contemplated the One True Reality. Having contemplated and perceived it, their defilements of sin were all extinguished; however, those who are icchantikas did not perceive it.
First, Icchantika Much-desire rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

My mind is shrouded in ignorance; although I have studied contemplation, I do not perceive the True Reality. From beginningless time until this very day, I have practiced the ten evil deeds exclusively. By what skillful means may I be enabled to see the True Reality and cause my transgressions to be eliminated?"
The Buddha said to Bahuruci:
"You icchantikas, all with one mind, I shall analyze and explain for you. Bahuruci!"
"You sentient beings should contemplate the Buddha-nature as being one within both body and mind; the Buddha-nature of the Dharma-body is one and not two.
If you can perform this contemplation of these two as one, it is called right contemplation, and it is also called the right view of the single characteristic."
If one perceives duality, it is called "false"; if one forms false views, afflictions arise.
If there are no false views, afflictions do not arise; if afflictions are severed, this is called "purity."
The Buddha said:
"All you sentient beings should single-mindedly contemplate the single Buddha-nature; beyond the Buddha-nature, nothing else is to be seen.
If there is anything seen, it is all false and illusory; to produce such illusions is to be inverted."
O you of many desires!

When the single mind is pure, then all phenomena are pure; when the single mind is defiled, then many phenomena are defiled. Defilement constitutes transgression, while purity constitutes the truth. If the mind is free from defilement, transgression will not arise.
Much-desire addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

From the distant past until this very day, I have committed immeasurable and boundless evil karmas throughout thousands of millions of kalpas. Having now resolved my mind and contemplated the single Buddha-nature and the reality of the True Dharma, will these boundless sins all be eliminated?"
"I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will explain this for me, so that my mind may become single-pointed and free from doubt.
The Buddha said,
"O you of great desire!"
If one contemplates the true reality, all transgressions are entirely eliminated.
Why is this? Because of excessive desire!
The defiled mind of the past is the pure mind of today; with a single mind there are no two, nor is there any other mind.
Since the mind is pure today, the mind of the past was also pure; therefore, one should know that all transgressions have been extinguished since incalculable kalpas ago.
It is like a dust-covered mirror from a thousand years ago that becomes bright as soon as it is brushed once with a cloth; all the dust is completely gone, leaving nothing behind.
It is also like a single torch lit in a dark room of a thousand years' standing, whereby all the darkness is entirely dispelled.
"You sentient beings!
You should always, with a single mind, contemplate the One True Reality (ekasatyatā), perform all dharmic practices within all phenomena, and depart from all worldly dharmas."
Why is this? Because of excessive desire!

All phenomena in the world, whether conditioned or unconditioned, are subject to decay. If these phenomena are subject to decay, then their activity is impermanent; if activity is impermanent, then phenomena arise and perish. To be free from the dharma of arising and perishing is what is called the True Truth (*satya*).

O you of many desires! It is like a potter who fashions various earthenware vessels; according to his will, the forms of these vessels are not fixed. The characteristics of these vessels, as well as their names, all arise and perish. Only the single nature of the clay is constant; all other physical forms are entirely subject to arising and perishing. This body of arising and perishing does not arise of itself; that which does not arise of itself is non-existent.
O you of great desire!
The Buddha-nature is like the clay, while the nature of sentient beings is like the vessel; this is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing.
If one is free from all karmic actions, that is the Buddha-body; by contemplating the single Buddha-body, one realizes there is no other karma.
Bahuśruta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I observe that all transgressions have been extinguished through the realization of the ultimate truths; what further karma must I perform to give birth to the Dharma-body?”
The Buddha told Bahudhātuka:
"If you contemplate the True Realities, all illnesses will not arise and both transgressions and defilements will be stilled; your mind will be like a vajra, ultimately indestructible;
you will be well able to uphold the precepts, and your mind will be like space, pure within and without."
Skillfully entering the meditative concentrations, the mind is like wind or fire, and all conditioned phenomena are utterly dispersed;
skillfully relying on wisdom is what is called liberation, and because of this liberation, one is able to know and see.
"Much-desiring one!
If you can practice this matter, you will immediately attain the fivefold Dharma-body.
Much-desiring addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the causes and effects of the fivefold Dharma-body?
The Buddha said:
"O you of great desire!
The Buddha-nature is the eternal cause, and the Dharma-body is the eternal fruit. Why is this so?"

The Buddha-nature of the causal mind attains its fruit through conditions; yet, when one is free from cause and free from fruit, there is neither cause nor fruit. This absence of cause and fruit is the true body of the Buddha. O you of many desires!

You should dwell in the tranquil purity of the pure land within the mind and contemplate with true mindfulness. Within this very mindfulness, one is born in the pure land and may preach the Dharma of Suchness for sentient beings. Entering the emptiness of the mind, one leaves behind all discursive speech; the three consciousnesses are of one nature, indestructible like a vajra.

At that time, there was another bodhisattva in the assembly named Wu-xing (Non-action). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—whether five hundred years, a thousand years, or fifteen hundred years have passed—one were to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, what Dharma should one preach?
"I pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will expound this for me so that I may be free from doubt.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Wu-xing:
"O son of good family!"

If, after fifteen hundred years, one preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, preaching the essence rather than the characteristics, and preaching the meaning rather than the words—such a preacher is truly preaching the Dharma.
If one speaks of the characteristics of words, moving the mouth and moving the mind, all of this is slander. Good son!
When preaching the Dharma to all sentient beings, you should speak according to the aspect of suchness and speak according to the aspect of equality.

Why is this? At that time, all sentient beings were afflicted by the same illness; because they shared one mind, one Buddha-nature, and the equality of all dharmas, to speak of superiority or inferiority therein would be called false speech, and their mouths shall be split and their tongues shall be torn asunder.
Why is this? Because the mental defilements of all sentient beings are one and the same defilement, and the mental purity of all sentient beings is one and the same purity. Why is this?
When the minds of all sentient beings are pure, they are equally pure through the ten wholesome dharmas;
when the minds of all sentient beings are defiled, they are equally defiled by the ten unwholesome [dharmas].
If sentient beings are ill, those who share the same illness require the same medicine; to preach many dharmas in such a case would be called inverted. Why is this?

Because they falsely discriminate between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas and thereby destroy all dharmas, and because they preach the Dharma according to their own biases, severing the path of the Buddha.
If a bodhisattva should preach the Dharma, they should preach it in accordance with the aspect of suchness (*tathatā*).
The Bodhisattva Wu-xing addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is the mark of suchness (tathatā-lakṣaṇa) explained?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Wu-xing, saying: “Good son!

To speak of the True Dharma of the single essence is to speak according to Suchness; to speak with a straightforward mind is to speak according to Suchness; to speak without partial attachment is to speak according to Suchness; to speak without discrimination is to speak according to Suchness; to speak while abiding in the single pure state of mind is to speak according to Suchness; and to speak that all speech is ineffable is to speak according to Suchness.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Apracāra, wishing to cause the entire assembly and all sentient beings to understand clearly, addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How is it that what is said to be ineffable is spoken of as being just as it is?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Wu-xing, saying: "Good son!
To speak of all dharmas as empty of their own characteristics is itself unspeakable;
to speak of all teachings as signless is itself unspeakable;
to speak of all dharmas as non-active is itself unspeakable.
“Good son! If one speaks in this manner, then it is not that which can be spoken; it is speaking in accordance with suchness.
The Bodhisattva Apracāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the Dharma is taught in this manner, how is it that the straightforward mind is fully explained?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Non-Action, saying:

“Good son! ‘Direct mind’ means that one directly believes in the meaning of the Tathāgata with the mind; it is not spoken according to one’s own mind. To be ‘complete’ means to be complete in the meaning of the ten wholesome paths, complete in the meaning of the four noble truths, complete in the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination, complete in the meaning of the six pāramitās, and complete in the meaning of the three gates of liberation. Being complete in such dharmas as these, one speaks of them as equal within a single mind, equal in the Buddha-nature, and equally pure—this is called ‘complete speech,’ and this is ‘speaking according to suchness.’”
Why is this? Because all dharmas are collectively one.
The Bodhisattva’s equal and pure dharma is like the taste of the great ocean water; though there are various kinds of precious jewels, all who seek them obtain them according to their own wishes.
It is like a single divine elixir, synthesized by blending various miscellaneous medicines together, which cures all diseases; whoever consumes it finds each and every ailment eliminated and healed.
It is the same for the one pure dharma, the one purity of mind, the one buddha-nature, and the one nature-pure dharma; because they are equal to all dharmas, to speak in this way is pure speech.
"If one were to speak of them separately, that would be a defiled teaching.

Why? Because all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; there is no one who lacks Buddha-nature. It is only that their awakening has degrees of distance and proximity, yet there is no distinction in the substance of the Dharma-body. Nevertheless, according to the fixed capacities of their faculties, one preaches the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle to those of the Lesser Vehicle, and the Dharma for icchantikas to those who are icchantikas."

If one speaks in such a manner, it is called not speaking the Dharma of the Buddha-way; this severs the Buddha-nature and extinguishes the Buddha-body. Such a person who speaks thus shall pass through hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas falling into the various hells, and even if a Buddha appears in the world, they shall not be able to escape.

Even if they should escape [from that state], should they be born among humans, they will be born in a remote borderland as low-born and destitute, where the Three Jewels do not exist; they will have cleft lips and no tongue, receiving such retribution.

Why is this? The nature of Bodhisattvas and sentient beings is the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). This Dharma-nature is eternally pure and endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*). From the very beginning, it is without gain or loss, without arising or ceasing; its nature is eternally real, devoid of falsehood and afflictions, and free from both nirvāṇa and increase or decrease. It is ultimately pure—a single nature of purity—which is itself the pure nature of bodhi.

The nature of bodhi is a single nature, non-dual, equal, and pure; it transcends the path of language and is like space. Being pure both internally and externally, it is a single purity that abides neither within nor without, nor in between. It is beyond words and speech; how, then, could one differentiate between illness and medicine therein?
If there is no conceptual discrimination, this is non-conceptual wisdom. "Good son!
Apart from the single mind, apart from the single purity, and apart from the single Buddha-nature, there is no Buddha to be sought, no Dharma to be taught, and no Sangha to be attained."

Why is this? Because the Buddha is the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Sangha; the Sangha is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and that which is unconditioned is the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and the Buddha-nature is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Therefore, I say that this sutra speaks only of one sentient being’s body, one mind, one purity, one Buddha-nature, one Buddha’s place of enlightenment, and one Bodhi tree, which fills all worlds and enters the bodies of all sentient beings.

“Good son! All Buddhas are born from this sutra; all dharmas are born from this sutra; the entire Sangha is seen through this sutra. Those who receive and uphold this sutra are said to receive and uphold the Triple Gem; those who contemplate this sutra are said to contemplate the Triple Gem; those who make offerings to this sutra are said to make offerings to the Triple Gem.”
The Bodhisattva Apracāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does one recollect the Three Jewels?”
“If one recollects the Triple Gem, how much merit does one obtain?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Wu Xing (Non-Action): “Good son!
If one contemplates the Three Jewels as being like empty space, their merit is immeasurable and inconceivable.

If one contemplates the Three Jewels as abiding in empty space, such that within the mind one does not even perceive the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha, this is the non-perception of all dharmas. Not perceiving all dharmas, one has no doubt regarding dharmas; contemplating the single true mark and the single essence of the Three Jewels within the state of purity—this is the contemplation of the Three Jewels.
The Bodhisattva Wu-xing addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Within the Three Jewels, one maintains single-minded right mindfulness; within the realm of afflictions, one’s own mind does not arise, nor does it arise in response to conditions; and regarding all wholesome dharmas, it is likewise so.”

Abiding in a single pure mind and relying on a single Buddha-nature, neither moving nor dwelling, and not taking this as the essence of dharmas; saving sentient beings as one would oneself, transforming all sentient beings as if transforming one's own body, and loving all sentient beings as one would protect one's own eyes—is this the practice of a bodhisattva, or is it not the practice of a bodhisattva?
“I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will explain this for me.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Wu-xing (Non-Practice):
“This is the practice of a bodhisattva.”
If one transforms sentient beings, one should cause them to uphold the mind rather than the words, and uphold practice rather than the teachings;
if one preaches the Dharma for them, one should speak of the meaning rather than the phrases, and speak of the meaning rather than the phrases.
Why is this? Because the Buddha-nature is the meaning. Why is this?
Because it is free from the characteristics of words.
To grasp at the characteristics of words is to fall into falsehood; to abandon the Buddha-nature is to lose the foundation. Good son!

If one seeks Buddhahood while having lost the Buddha-nature, it is like attempting to cure a person's illness within a shadow, like trying to produce fire by rubbing ice, or like a wingless bird intending to fly high; in the end, the Dharma cannot be attained.

“Good son! Within this sutra, you should discipline the mind to grasp the meaning; you must not follow the literal words but should instead grasp the underlying principle. If one does not grasp the principle, it is called falsehood. Furthermore, one must not misapprehend the characteristic of emptiness within that principle to convert sentient beings; such a person is termed an icchantika with the view of emptiness.”

It is simply that one causes sentient beings, within a single mind, to contemplate and know that the single Buddha-nature truly exists. This characteristic of true existence neither resides in existence nor in non-existence; by contemplating this wondrous Suchness as it truly is, one should immediately settle the mind and abide in this state.
If one abides in this state, it is called purity.
In this state of purity, to abide is to have no foundation, and to abide is itself movement.
"Therefore, all Buddhas and Tathāgatas establish all dharmas from the place of no-origination.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Non-action (Acarita), wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Great Sage, the Honored Buddha, Desiring to enter the tranquility of Nirvāṇa, For the sake of delivering sentient beings,"
I speak this sutra of the true One Vehicle.
Dwelling in the ground of compassion, out of pity for sentient beings, I inquire of the Buddha regarding the intent of the One Vehicle within the definitive teachings.
The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is entirely detached from the world; entering into reality, he speaks of the Buddha-nature, wherein all phenomena are pure.
Detached from words and detached from characteristics, it abides neither within nor without; though spoken of, it cannot be spoken—therefore it is called the "Suchness of Speech.
Thus, the Dharma of equality dwells in a single nature; this single nature, the pure Dharma, is fundamentally without arising or ceasing.
Within emptiness and non-emptiness, the wondrous nature is eternally without substance; liberation is neither liberation nor non-liberation, for it is fundamentally pure and unstained.
All defilements are fundamentally unattached; False attachment is like mud and filth. This mud is what constitutes the stain, For the wondrous nature is eternally pure.
In purity there is nothing to be purified, And in defilement there is nothing to be stained. The nature of mud is itself the impurity, Yet the nature of that impurity is primordially empty.

The nature of defilement resembles mad flowers: though they fall from the tree, it remains as before; the nature of the tree is without arising or ceasing, while the mad flowers come and go of their own accord.
The Buddha-nature is fundamentally unborn, Transcending all states of arising and ceasing; There is neither motion nor stillness, For its nature is eternally thus.
It is both one and not one, Not named, yet not unspeakable; Furthermore, it is free from all views, Where there is no seeing, yet it is visible.
Because of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, seeing is itself bodhi; this wondrous enlightened nature of bodhi is unmoving and has nothing to be awakened to.
This is precisely the body of sentient beings: one mind, one Buddha-nature; one Buddha, one site of enlightenment;
one great Bodhi tree. It can fill the realm of empty space and universally enter the bodies of all sentient beings.
Within the true Triple Gem, all are one and without duality; they do not abide in the realm of form and substance, nor do they dwell at the limit of emptiness.
Entering into the sphere of false existence, they ultimately rest in the abode of quiescent voidness.
"Originally without a fundamental locus, yet establishing all dharmas; teaching and transforming all sentient beings, causing them to enter the Tathāgatagarbha.

At that time, having seen the Bodhisattva Wu-xing (Non-action) finish reciting these verses, the Buddha immediately, by means of his supernatural power, emitted a great radiance that pervaded the trichiliocosm.
Within that radiance, the pure lands of the ten directions appeared; all those lands were utterly adorned and purified, complete with every kind of garden, grove, pond, and pool.

Within the waters of those ponds were lotus pedestals of five colors, and upon each individual flower was a great city. Within each great city was a single pure mahāmaṇi jewel, and within each great mahāmaṇi jewel was a Tathāgata’s seat, accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty people.

All those Buddhas, for the sake of the great assembly, expound the Dharma of the Single Vehicle, causing all sentient beings to abide with an unmoving mind within a single body, a single Buddha, a single nature, and a single state of purity; they do not take conditions from external objects nor enter into various forms of knowledge; their minds are like space, unstained by anything; their minds are like adamant, indestructible regarding all precepts; their minds are like the waters of the ocean, constantly flowing with wisdom; and they all attain liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, and the fivefold Dharma-body.

At that time, the Bodhisattva A-practice (Acarin), the great assembly, and all sentient beings, having seen this event, were filled with great joy; they all dwelt in single-minded concentration, no longer conditioned by anything, and entered the state of purity.
The Buddha then withdrew his light and addressed the great assembly, saying: "O practitioners!
I wish to enter the tranquility of nirvana; the time is drawing near."

If, after my parinirvāṇa, during this age of the five turbidities, there are those who, within this sutra, practice contemplation as described—contemplating the single body-mind, dwelling not in any evils and not departing from bodhi—they will certainly attain liberation and realize the path of the One Vehicle.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Wu-xing, saying:
“If, after my parinirvāṇa, one should encounter this sutra and hear its meaning during the evil age of the five turbidities, that person is as if they have met the Buddha.”

If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be a person who can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, practicing according to its teachings with an unshakable mind, untainted by any defilements and transcending all traces of dust; and if, moreover, they cause other sentient beings to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and further explain its meaning to instruct them—then although such a person is but an ordinary being, they are a bodhisattva who roars like a lion.

At that time, there was another bodhisattva in the assembly named Dharmarāja. He rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, withdrew to stand to one side, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, in this Jambudvīpa during the evil age of the five turbidities, I shall teach and transform sentient beings by preaching this excellent medicine to cure all their illnesses, causing them all to be healed;
furthermore, with the diamond-wisdom blade of this sutra, I shall cut away the ignorance of all sentient beings;
and furthermore, with the pure Dharma-staff of this sutra, I shall lash away and remove the defilements of the three poisons from sentient beings.
Furthermore, by means of the great wisdom-power of this sutra, the Hero, one shall liberate sentient beings from the bonds of the ten entanglements (*paryavasthāna*);
furthermore, by means of the great wisdom-boat of this sutra, one shall ferry sentient beings across to reach the other shore;

furthermore, by means of the dharma of the single nature and purity of this sutra, one shall cause all sentient beings to attain a single body, a single mind, a single Buddha, a single nature, and a single purity, so that they definitively enter the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and definitively emerge from hell.
World-Honored One!
If I am unable to save sentient beings and cause them to enter the various hells, that would be the extinction of my Buddha-body.
I only pray that the World-Honored One [will grant me this].

Entrusting this Buddha-dharma to me, please explain it further for my sake so that I may extensively deliver sentient beings, enabling them to understand much from hearing little and know much from seeing little; that they do not seek voluminous texts to grasp the meaning, but rather attain certain liberation within a few teachings, free from all doubt and remainder.
“I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will expound this for me.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:

“This Bodhisattva Dharmarāja has already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas over the course of kalpas; he is skillful in means to rescue and deliver sentient beings. This Bodhisattva is able to sustain the lives of sentient beings by means of the constant wind of a single flavor.”
"You sentient beings and those of the future!

If you should uphold the names of these bodhisattvas, and further cause great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to recite this sutra and extensively explain its meaning, then any illnesses shall be entirely eliminated, and no malevolent beasts or spirits will be able to approach you."

“Bodhisattva! Since you possess such benefit for sentient beings, I entrust this sutra to you. I shall also explain to you the method for saving and delivering sentient beings: hear little yet understand much; see little yet know much; do not seek voluminous texts merely to grasp the meaning.”
"All of you Bodhisattvas, listen with single-minded attention; I shall proclaim it for you.
All sentient beings are of one mind, one Buddha, and one nature; all afflictions arise from the single mind, all originating through the conditions of the two spheres of object and wisdom."

Why is this? Because the two kinds of nature—the nature of conditions and the nature of self-substance—arise through the power of these two natures; these two kinds of power-nature arise from the deluded mind of a single thought-moment, and this deluded mind has no fundamental basis.
If a single thought stirs, afflictions immediately arise; one should contemplate this thought and recognize it as the deluded mind.
This deluded mind has no foundation, and having no foundation means there is no abiding. If one knows there is no abiding, then awakening arises within the mind.

Because the primordially awakened pure mind is free from conceptual thought, if the mind is free from thought, it is immovable; if the mind is immovable, there is also no abiding mind—this is called purity.
The essence of the pure empty mind is intrinsically pure; there is no purity to be realized, for it is detached from all notions of purification, and thus it is called "pure.

Within this pure mind, the Bodhisattva is without action, without arising, without defilement, without purity, without increase, and without decrease. Ultimately unstained, not residing in any single place, and transcending names and numbers, it is both eternal and non-eternal. Like a diamond, its singular nature is indestructible; like space, it accommodates all things; and like a lotus, it is unsullied by the waters of craving. If one practices in this manner, one will certainly attain liberation, transcending birth and death and emerging from the suffering of the hells.
This single-minded dharma of the bodhisattva is called: first, liberation through repentance, because one perceives the true essence;
second, liberation through the practice of the Dharma, because one abides in a single place;
third, liberation through non-practice, because there is no dwelling or attachment.
"These three liberations are all produced within a single mind, because all sentient beings do not possess two minds, and because all sentient beings are of the One Vehicle.
The Buddha said to Dharmarāja Bodhisattva: "Good son!"
If one can know a single dharma, one should know all dharmas; if one does not know a single dharma, one does not know all dharmas.
Why is this? Because there is no dharma that does not possess the single characteristic [of emptiness].
If a bodhisattva hears this "one," that is merely having heard little; to know no dharma that is not known is called "vast understanding.
Why is this? Because the nature of all dharmas returns to the single purity.
To see this one is to see the bodies of all Buddhas. Why is this?
All Buddha-bodies arise from a single place of purity; this single ground of purity is the body of all Buddhas, the site of enlightenment for all Buddhas, and the Bodhi tree of all Buddhas.
“Good son! Within this Dharma, one cuts off all afflictions just as one fells a tree: one merely cuts the single root without cutting the branches and leaves. Why is this?

It is, for example, like a person whose body has been struck by a poisoned arrow; as long as they experience pain in the body, if the arrow is immediately extracted, the pain will be removed, but if the arrow is not extracted, the pain will not cease.
He asked, "What kind of bird's feathers are on these arrows?
He further asked, "From which mountain does this bamboo originate?
And he further asked, "Whose archery is this arrow?"
This person’s pain was such that his life had already ended; yet, even if one were to extract the arrow, it would ultimately be known to be of no benefit.
"Good son! If the mind has impurities, one should immediately purify the mind."
If the mind is in a state of purity, it is called "pure.
All teachings on purity state that by being free from all forms of grasping, one can enter into non-grasping. Why is this?
It is without origin and without abode, because it is eternal, blissful, self, and pure;
it is without origin and without abode, for True Suchness (tathatā) is real and never apart from all things, being fundamentally detached even from detachment;
its nature is not separate from the locus of the Path, as it dwells in non-dwelling; it is equal to the mind, being one and without distinction or duality.
It does not abide in a permanent location, for it is fundamentally uninterrupted;
it neither moves nor dwells, for its nature is eternally one. Yet even this "one" is not one, for it is free from names and numbers.

“Good son! Just as the great tree remains ever-stable and unmoved by the six winds, so too does the single-natured diamond not give rise to dualistic views. Being neither existent nor non-existent, one dwells in the wondrous, eternal emptiness. With the sword of wisdom, which is unborn, one cuts through all afflictions; with the unimpeded understanding of emptiness, one subdues one’s own mind, such that the demon king does not arise and hostile thieves do not emerge.”
“Good son! In this Dharma, those who seek the true substance do not plant branches or leaves, but cultivate only the root; if it sprouts, flowers and fruits will emerge of their own accord.”
This minor teaching of mine is likewise so: it is like the āmalaka fruit; by planting a single fruit, one obtains fruits without end.
I declare this Dharma to be the foremost among all dharmas and the Great Vehicle King among all vehicles; therefore, this sutra is named "The Dharma King.
Furthermore, because this sutra is entrusted to the Bodhisattva Dharmarāja, it is also named "The Dharma King."
You, the great assembly who uphold this sutra, shall immediately be liberated from all calamities. If you are to uphold it, do so wherever you may be. Why is this?

The Buddha-nature is eternally within the mind, ever empty and quiescent; internal dhyāna is the true, pure Vajra; the six sense-bases are the city gates of the eternal Suchness-realm (tathatā-dhātu); whether one is present or absent, one abides within the realm of emptiness.
"You, the great assembly, must all remain silent; the time is drawing near for me to enter parinirvāṇa. This sutra is titled 'The Nirvāṇa-Adornment Prajñāpāramitā Unhindered Liberation.'"
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the great assembly all attained the emptiness and liberation of the *prajñāpāramitā* of nirvāṇa, free from obstruction.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmarāja rose from where he had prostrated himself and immediately entered great nirvāṇa at that very spot. He realized the liberation of emptiness in the stage of non-attachment; whether lifting his foot or setting it down, he moved through purity. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he paid homage and departed.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-King Spoken by the Buddha, one fascicle.
